payload.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
payload.holding: The court held that the insurance companies were jointly and severally liable with the owners to satisfy the third-party claims despite the drivers' licences not being current on the exact date of the accidents, and enhanced the compensation awarded in both claim cases while reducing the interest rate to 9% per annum.
payload.ratio: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence, and the mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability.

payload.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
payload.holding: The High Court dismissed the insurance company's appeal, confirming the judgment and award passed by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal granting compensation of Rs. 4,17,500/- with interest.
payload.ratio: In motor accident claims, the burden of proving contributory negligence lies on the party asserting it, and where an insurer is already impleaded as a party respondent, it can contest the claim on all available grounds without being restricted to statutory defences under Section 149(2) regardless of whether an application under Section 170 was rejected.

alling under the age group of 31 to 35 years is '17'. Learned MACT correctly chosen the
multiplier '17' and, thus, worked out the total compensation amount as Rs. 4,08,000/-. Further, as
per guidelines of Hon'ble Supreme Court, Rs. 2000/- for the cremation, Rs. 25,00/- for the loss of
estate and Rs. 5000/-, also added by the tribunal for the loss of concert, was granted to the
widow-the claim petitioner. The interest is also awarded at the proper rate of 7% per annum,

chargeable from the date of petition till the date of actual payment. As such the amount worked out
by the tribunal as compensation to be awarded to the claim-petitioners is not excessive. The ground
taken in the appeal in this regard and the argument made is baseless.
18. Learned counsel for the offending Truck No. 44 AH/4081 has cited the judgment rendered in the
case of New India Assurance Company Ltd. Vs. Salma Begum reported in [2014(4) T.A.C. 630 (All.)]
which relates to the quantum of compensation. The law given in the case of Sarla Verma by the Apex
Court for determination of compensation has been adopted by Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of
National Insurance Company Limited Vs. Pranay Sethi and Others reported in [AIR 2017, Supreme
Court 5157].
19. So far as the excessive award of amount of compensation is concerned, the argument is quite
baseless as the learned Motor Accident Claims Tribunal did not rely simply on the oral evidence of
the claim-petitioners regarding the monthly income having been earned by the deceased from taxi
driving @ Rs. 5000/- per month but notionally fixed Rs. 3000/- per month taking income Rs. 100/-
per day as per then prevailing rate of minimum wages on notional basis and determined the
compensation taking help of guidelines given by Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Sarla Verma
(supra).

args.question: What rates of interest have been awarded on motor accident compensation, and from which date does interest run?
args.answer:
## Interest Rates Awarded on Motor Accident Compensation

Based on the corpus of 56 judgments, the following interest rates have been awarded:

### 1. 9% per annum (most common rate)
- **doc_022** — *Sangeeta Devi v. Mahesh Chand & Ors.* (MACT, Delhi, 2018): Awarded interest @ 9% p.a. on the total compensation amount **from the date of filing of the petition till realization**.
- **doc_041** — *No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased...* (MACT, Bangalore, 2016): Awarded compensation with interest @ 9% p.a. **from the date of the petition till the date of payment**.
- **doc_010** — *Raju Gupta v. Himachal Road* (MACT, Delhi, 2018): Awarded interest @ 9% p.a. **from the date of filing of petition till realization**.
- **doc_034** — *K.G. Srinivasamurthy v. Habib Khathun* (MACT, Madhugiri, 2001): Reduced interest from 12% to **9% p.a. from the date of petition to the date of payment**, following the Supreme Court in *Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd.*, which held that in view of the change in economy and RBI policy, 9% is reasonable.

### 2. 7.5% per annum
- **doc_023** — *Suman Lata v. Madan Mohan Sonkar* (MACT, Faizabad, 2005): Reduced interest from 9% to **7.5% p.a.**, following *Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corporation v. Section Raj Priya* (2005) where the Supreme Court allowed 7.5% "keeping in view the Bank rate."

### 3. 7% per annum
- **doc_018** — *Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Smt. Rani & Ors.* (Allahabad High Court, 2019): Confirmed the Tribunal's award of interest @ **7% per annum, payable from the date of application (petition) till actual payment**.

### 4. 6% per annum
- **doc_004** — *Oriental Insurance Co. v. Soma Devi* (Himachal Pradesh High Court, 2020): Reduced interest from 7.5% to **6% per annum, retrospectively from the date of filing of the petition**. The Court observed: *"There is a trend of falling interest rates and these are likely to fall unless we catch up the global rates of interest, which are quite low. The prevalent interest rates are around 5%."*

### 5. 12% per annum (reduced on appeal)
- **doc_034** — *K.G. Srinivasamurthy v. Habib Khathun*: The Tribunal had originally awarded 12% p.a., but this was reduced to 9% on appeal.

---

## Date from Which Interest Runs

Across all judgments in the corpus, the consistent position is that **interest runs from the date of filing of the claim petition** (not from the date of the accident). The formulations used are:

| Formulation | Examples |
|---|---|
| "from the date of filing of petition till realization" | doc_022, doc_010 |
| "from the date of petition till the date of payment" | doc_041, doc_034 |
| "from the date of filing of the petition" (retrospectively) | doc_004 |
| "from the date of application till actual payment" | doc_018 |

No judgment in this corpus awarded interest from the date of the accident itself; the starting point is uniformly the date the claimant approached the Tribunal.

---

## Summary Table

| Rate | Judgment | Year | Court | Starting Point |
|------|----------|------|-------|---------------|
| **9% p.a.** | doc_022 (Sangeeta Devi) | 2018 | MACT Delhi | Date of filing |
| **9% p.a.** | doc_041 (Mother of deceased) | 2016 | MACT Bangalore | Date of petition |
| **9% p.a.** | doc_010 (Raju Gupta) | 2018 | MACT Delhi | Date of filing |
| **9% p.a.** | doc_034 (K.G. Srinivasamurthy) | 2001 | MACT Madhugiri | Date of petition |
| **7.5% p.a.** | doc_023 (Suman Lata) | 2005 | MACT Faizabad | (not specified but consistent) |
| **7% p.a.** | doc_018 (Oriental v. Rani) | 2019 | Allahabad HC | Date of application |
| **6% p.a.** | doc_004 (Oriental v. Soma Devi) | 2020 | Himachal HC | Date of filing |

The trend over time shows a **declining trajectory**: 12% (reduced to 9% in 2001) → 9% (common in 2005–2018) → 7.5% (2005) → 7% (2019) → 6% (2020), reflecting the general fall in bank interest rates and the economic policy of the Reserve Bank of India.

adverse.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
adverse.principle: Interest at 6% per annum is appropriate given falling interest rates; the court reduced interest from 7.5% to 6% retrospectively from the date of filing.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this 2020 Himachal Pradesh High Court judgment to argue that interest rates should be reduced to 6% (or even lower) because 'prevalent interest rates are around 5%'. This is the most recent judgment on point in the corpus and represents a downward trend.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a single High Court judgment, not a Supreme Court ruling. The Supreme Court in Kaushnuma Begum (cited in doc_034) held 9% reasonable, and Pranay Sethi did not disturb that. The Soma Devi court's observation that rates 'are likely to fall unless we catch up the global rates' is speculative and not binding on other courts. Claimants can argue that 9% remains the settled norm and that a single High Court cannot override the Supreme Court's guidance.
adverse.quote: There is a trend of falling interest rates and these are likely to fall unless we catch up the global rates of interest, which are quite low. The prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum, retrospectively, i.e. from the date of the filing of the petition.

adverse.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
adverse.principle: Interest at 7.5% per annum is sufficient; 9% is excessive.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this to argue that even 9% is too high and should be reduced to 7.5%, relying on the Supreme Court's decision in Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corporation v. Section Raj Priya.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a 2005 MACT decision, not a binding Supreme Court precedent on the rate itself. The Supreme Court in Raj Priya allowed 7.5% in the specific facts of that case but did not lay down 7.5% as a universal cap. Claimants can argue that 9% has been consistently awarded by numerous tribunals and High Courts (docs 022, 041, 010, 034) and remains the standard.
adverse.quote: Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corporation ltd. v. Section Raj Priya and Ors. ... keeping in view the Bank rate the interest was allowed @ 7.5% per annum only. In view of the above, we are of the view that the interest should be reduced to 7.5% per annum.

adverse.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
adverse.principle: Interest at 7% per annum is a 'proper rate'.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this Allahabad High Court judgment to argue that 7% is judicially approved as 'proper', supporting a reduction from 9%.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court in doc_018 did not engage in any detailed analysis of the interest rate — it merely stated that the rate was 'proper' in a single sentence. It is not a considered ruling on the appropriate rate and carries less weight than the Supreme Court's guidance in Kaushnuma Begum endorsing 9%.
adverse.quote: The interest is also awarded at the proper rate of 7% per annum, chargeable from the date of petition till the date of actual payment.

priority_arguments: Lead with Kaushnuma Begum (via doc_034) — the Supreme Court has held that 9% is reasonable given RBI policy and bank rates, and this remains good law.
Point to the consistent pattern: 9% was awarded in 2001 (doc_034), 2016 (doc_041), and 2018 (docs 022, 010) — this is the settled rate across multiple tribunals and states.
Argue that the 6% rate in Soma Devi (doc_004) is an outlier from a single High Court judge, not binding precedent, and contradicts the Supreme Court's view in Kaushnuma Begum.
Emphasise that interest uniformly runs from the date of filing of the petition (not the accident date) — this is consistent across all judgments and should not be disturbed.

If the insurer argues for a lower rate, counter that the claimant should not bear the risk of fluctuating economic conditions; the compensation is meant to be 'just' and the rate should reflect the claimant's loss of use of the money, not the bank's deposit rate.
strategy.compensation_range: Interest at 9% per annum from the date of filing of the petition till realization is the most strongly supported position. If the court follows the downward trend, 7.5% or 7% is possible. 6% is the floor based on this corpus but is the least likely outcome given it is a single High Court judgment.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The corpus shows a clear hierarchy: 9% (most common, supported by Kaushnuma Begum SC authority) > 7.5% (supported by Raj Priya SC) > 7% (Allahabad HC) > 6% (Himachal HC). The starting date is uniformly the date of filing of the petition, not the accident date.
risks: The Himachal Pradesh High Court in Soma Devi (doc_004, 2020) reduced interest to 6%, and insurers will aggressively cite this as the most recent authority on point.
The general downward trend in interest rates may influence courts to reduce rates further, especially if the matter is heard in 2025-26.
If the claimant delayed filing the petition, the insurer may argue that interest should run from a later date or at a reduced rate.
Some courts may treat the interest rate as discretionary and not bound by precedent, leading to unpredictability.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Claimants should seek 9% per annum from the date of filing of the petition till realization, citing Kaushnuma Begum (via doc_034) and the consistent line of MACT decisions (docs 022, 041, 010). If the insurer cites Soma Devi (doc_004), distinguish it as a non-binding High Court decision that contradicts Supreme Court authority.

caveats: The corpus does not contain any Supreme Court judgment directly ruling on the interest rate post-Pranay Sethi (2017). The most recent judgment in the corpus is Soma Devi (2020, Himachal HC) which reduced rates to 6%. Practitioners should check for any Supreme Court ruling after 2020 on this point.

None of the judgments in the corpus discuss interest on the enhanced portion of compensation separately (i.e., whether interest on the enhanced amount runs from the date of the claim petition or from the date of the appellate order). This may be relevant in appeal scenarios.
The corpus does not contain any judgment awarding interest at a rate higher than 9% (the original 12% in doc_034 was reduced). Claimants seeking more than 9% will find no support in this corpus.

args.question: What rates of interest have been awarded on motor accident compensation, and from which date does interest run?

supporting.title: Sangeeta Devi W/O Sh. Vinod Kumar Singh vs Mahesh Chand & Ors
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% per annum from the date of filing of petition till realization is the standard rate awarded by MACTs.
supporting.fact_alignment: Standard MACT award where the tribunal awarded 9% p.a. from the date of filing — the most common formulation in the corpus.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes 9% as the benchmark rate that claimants can expect, with interest running from the date of petition.
supporting.quote: Claimant is also entitled to the interest @ 09% p.a. on the total compensation amount from the date of filing of petition till realization.

supporting.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1 Has Filed The Written Statement To ...
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% per annum from the date of petition till payment is the standard rate.
supporting.fact_alignment: A 2016 MACT Bangalore judgment awarding 9% p.a. from the date of petition — consistent with the prevailing rate.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces 9% as the standard rate applied by tribunals across jurisdictions.
supporting.quote: The Petitioners are entitled for compensation of Rupees 25,95,346/- with interest at the rate of 9% p.a. from the date of the petition till the date of payment.

supporting.title: Raju Gupta S/O Sh. Madan Mohan Gupta vs Himachal Road
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% per annum from the date of filing of petition till realization.
supporting.fact_alignment: A 2018 MACT Delhi judgment awarding 9% p.a. from the date of filing — consistent pattern.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows continuity of the 9% rate in Delhi MACTs as late as 2018.
supporting.quote: Claimant is also entitled to the interest @ 09% p.a. on the total compensation amount from the date of filing of petition till realization.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% per annum from the date of petition is reasonable, reducing from 12%, following Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. (SC).
supporting.fact_alignment: The court reduced interest from 12% to 9% citing the Supreme Court's view in Kaushnuma Begum that 9% is reasonable given RBI policy and bank rates.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the Supreme Court authority (Kaushnuma Begum) for 9% as the appropriate rate, and shows that 12% was considered excessive even in 2001.
supporting.quote: The Apex Court in Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. has held that, in view of the change in the economy and policy of Reserve Bank of India and the prevalent rate of interest for the fixed deposit by the nationalised banks, it would be reasonable to award interest at 9 per cent per annum.

supporting.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
supporting.principle: Interest at 7.5% per annum is appropriate, reducing from 9%, following the Supreme Court in Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corporation v. Section Raj Priya.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court reduced interest from 9% to 7.5% citing the Supreme Court's decision which considered the prevailing bank rate.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that even 9% can be reduced where the Supreme Court has indicated a lower rate based on bank rates.
supporting.quote: Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corporation ltd. v. Section Raj Priya and Ors. ... keeping in view the Bank rate the interest was allowed @ 7.5% per annum only. In view of the above, we are of the view that the interest should be reduced to 7.5% per annum.

supporting.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
supporting.principle: Interest at 7% per annum from the date of application till actual payment is a 'proper rate'.
supporting.fact_alignment: The Allahabad High Court confirmed the Tribunal's award of 7% p.a. from the date of application (petition) till actual payment.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that 7% is also judicially approved by a High Court as a proper rate.
supporting.quote: The interest is also awarded at the proper rate of 7% per annum, chargeable from the date of petition till the date of actual payment.

adverse.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
adverse.principle: Interest at 6% per annum is appropriate given falling interest rates; the court reduced interest from 7.5% to 6% retrospectively from the date of filing.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this 2020 Himachal Pradesh High Court judgment to argue that interest rates should be reduced to 6% (or even lower) because 'prevalent interest rates are around 5%'. This is the most recent judgment on point in the corpus and represents a downward trend.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a single High Court judgment, not a Supreme Court ruling. The Supreme Court in Kaushnuma Begum (cited in doc_034) held 9% reasonable, and Pranay Sethi did not disturb that. The Soma Devi court's observation that rates 'are likely to fall unless we catch up the global rates' is speculative and not binding on other courts. Claimants can argue that 9% remains the settled norm.
adverse.quote: There is a trend of falling interest rates and these are likely to fall unless we catch up the global rates of interest, which are quite low. The prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum, retrospectively, i.e. from the date of the filing of the petition.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Interest at 6% per annum from the date of petition is proper, following the Karnataka High Court's view in Vijay Ishwar Jadhav that Section 34 CPC limits interest to 6% in MACT matters.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this 2024 MACT Bangalore judgment as the most recent authority in the corpus. It directly holds that under Section 34 CPC, interest at more than 6% could not have been awarded in MACT proceedings, relying on the Karnataka High Court's decision in Vijay Ishwar Jadhav. This is a powerful argument for capping interest at 6%.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The Vijay Ishwar Jadhav line of authority is specific to Karnataka and is not universally accepted. Other High Courts and the Supreme Court (Kaushnuma Begum) have endorsed 9%. Section 34 CPC applies to civil courts; MACTs are tribunals under the Motor Vehicles Act, and Section 149(1) of the MV Act itself contemplates interest. The argument that Section 34 CPC caps MACT interest is contested and not settled law across all jurisdictions.
adverse.quote: The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in M.F.A. 13390/2014 ... has elaborately discussed with regard to the rate of interest ... wherein at para No.15 it is held that '... the provisions of Section 34 of C.P.C. to that extent become invocable ... Therefore, in the absence of any other law relating to interest on judgments, the MACT has to follow the provisions of Section 34 of C.P.C., 1908. Thus, in the given circumstances of this case, interest at the rate of more than 6% could not have been awarded.'

adverse.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
adverse.principle: Interest at 7.5% per annum is sufficient; 9% is excessive, following the Supreme Court in Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corporation v. Section Raj Priya.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this to argue that even 9% is too high and should be reduced to 7.5%, relying on a Supreme Court decision (Raj Priya) that allowed 7.5% keeping in view the bank rate.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Raj Priya did not lay down 7.5% as a universal cap — it was a fact-specific decision. Claimants can argue that 9% has been consistently awarded by numerous tribunals and High Courts (docs 022, 041, 010, 034) and remains the standard. The Kaushnuma Begum SC authority endorsing 9% is also binding.
adverse.quote: Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corporation ltd. v. Section Raj Priya and Ors. ... keeping in view the Bank rate the interest was allowed @ 7.5% per annum only. In view of the above, we are of the view that the interest should be reduced to 7.5% per annum.

adverse.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
adverse.principle: Interest at 7% per annum is a 'proper rate'.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this Allahabad High Court judgment to argue that 7% is judicially approved as 'proper', supporting a reduction from 9%.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court in doc_018 did not engage in any detailed analysis of the interest rate — it merely stated that the rate was 'proper' in a single sentence. It is not a considered ruling on the appropriate rate and carries less weight than the Supreme Court's guidance in Kaushnuma Begum endorsing 9%.
adverse.quote: The interest is also awarded at the proper rate of 7% per annum, chargeable from the date of petition till the date of actual payment.

priority_arguments: Lead with Kaushnuma Begum (via doc_034) — the Supreme Court has held that 9% is reasonable given RBI policy and bank rates, and this remains good law.
Point to the consistent pattern: 9% was awarded in 2001 (doc_034), 2016 (doc_041), and 2018 (docs 022, 010) — this is the settled rate across multiple tribunals and states.
Argue that the 6% rate in Soma Devi (doc_004) is an outlier from a single High Court judge, not binding precedent, and contradicts the Supreme Court's view in Kaushnuma Begum.
Distinguish doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) as a Karnataka-specific MACT decision applying Section 34 CPC — this is not the law across all states and is contrary to the weight of authority.
Emphasise that interest uniformly runs from the date of filing of the petition (not the accident date) — this is consistent across all judgments and should not be disturbed.

If the insurer argues for a lower rate, counter that the claimant should not bear the risk of fluctuating economic conditions; the compensation is meant to be 'just' and the rate should reflect the claimant's loss of use of the money, not the bank's deposit rate.
strategy.compensation_range: Interest at 9% per annum from the date of filing of the petition till realization is the most strongly supported position. If the court follows the downward trend, 7.5% or 7% is possible. 6% is the floor based on this corpus but is the least likely outcome given it is contradicted by Supreme Court authority.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The corpus shows a hierarchy: 9% (most common, supported by Kaushnuma Begum SC) > 7.5% (supported by Raj Priya SC) > 7% (Allahabad HC) > 6% (Himachal HC and Karnataka MACT). The starting date is uniformly the date of filing of the petition, not the accident date.
risks: The Himachal Pradesh High Court in Soma Devi (doc_004, 2020) reduced interest to 6%, and insurers will aggressively cite this as the most recent High Court authority on point.

The Karnataka High Court's Vijay Ishwar Jadhav line (applied in doc_024, 2024) holds that Section 34 CPC caps MACT interest at 6% — this is the most recent judgment in the corpus and directly adverse.
The general downward trend in interest rates may influence courts to reduce rates further, especially if the matter is heard in 2025-26.
If the claimant delayed filing the petition, the insurer may argue that interest should run from a later date or at a reduced rate.
Some courts may treat the interest rate as discretionary and not bound by precedent, leading to unpredictability.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Claimants should seek 9% per annum from the date of filing of the petition till realization, citing Kaushnuma Begum (via doc_034) and the consistent line of MACT decisions (docs 022, 041, 010). If the insurer cites Soma Devi (doc_004) or Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024), distinguish them as non-binding High Court/MACT decisions that contradict Supreme Court authority. In Karnataka, the Vijay Ishwar Jadhav precedent creates a specific risk that requires separate briefing.

caveats: doc_001 (United India Insurance v. Neelam Devi, 2023, Punjab & Haryana HC) — outcome 'mixed'. This judgment deals with income assessment methodology (DC rates vs minimum wages) and pay-and-recover rights for licence defects. It does not discuss interest rates at all and is irrelevant to the interest rate question.

doc_014 (Shivlal v. Rukmabai, 1985, MP HC) — outcome 'insurer'. This judgment deals with gratuitous passenger liability under the 1939 Motor Vehicles Act. It does not discuss interest rates and is irrelevant to the interest rate question.
The corpus does not contain any Supreme Court judgment directly ruling on the interest rate post-Pranay Sethi (2017). Practitioners should check for any Supreme Court ruling after 2020 on this point.

None of the judgments in the corpus discuss interest on the enhanced portion of compensation separately (i.e., whether interest on the enhanced amount runs from the date of the claim petition or from the date of the appellate order). This may be relevant in appeal scenarios.

The corpus does not contain any judgment awarding interest at a rate higher than 9% (the original 12% in doc_034 was reduced on appeal). Claimants seeking more than 9% will find no support in this corpus.

supporting.fact_alignment: The Allahabad High Court confirmed the Tribunal's award of 7% p.a. from the date of application (petition) till actual payment.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that 7% is also judicially approved by a High Court as a proper rate.
supporting.quote: The interest is also awarded at the proper rate of 7% per annum, chargeable from the date of petition till the date of actual payment.

adverse.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
adverse.principle: Interest at 6% per annum is appropriate given falling interest rates; the court reduced interest from 7.5% to 6% retrospectively from the date of filing.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this 2020 Himachal Pradesh High Court judgment to argue that interest rates should be reduced to 6% (or even lower) because 'prevalent interest rates are around 5%'. This is the most recent judgment on point in the corpus and represents a downward trend.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a single High Court judgment, not a Supreme Court ruling. The Supreme Court in Kaushnuma Begum (cited in doc_034) held 9% reasonable, and Pranay Sethi did not disturb that. The Soma Devi court's observation that rates 'are likely to fall unless we catch up the global rates' is speculative and not binding on other courts. Claimants can argue that 9% remains the settled norm.
adverse.quote: There is a trend of falling interest rates and these are likely to fall unless we catch up the global rates of interest, which are quite low. The prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum, retrospectively, i.e. from the date of the filing of the petition.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Interest at 6% per annum from the date of petition is proper, following the Karnataka High Court's view in Vijay Ishwar Jadhav that Section 34 CPC limits interest to 6% in MACT matters.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this 2024 MACT Bangalore judgment as the most recent authority in the corpus. It directly holds that under Section 34 CPC, interest at more than 6% could not have been awarded in MACT proceedings, relying on the Karnataka High Court's decision in Vijay Ishwar Jadhav. This is a powerful argument for capping interest at 6%.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The Vijay Ishwar Jadhav line of authority is specific to Karnataka and is not universally accepted. Other High Courts and the Supreme Court (Kaushnuma Begum) have endorsed 9%. Section 34 CPC applies to civil courts; MACTs are tribunals under the Motor Vehicles Act, and Section 149(1) of the MV Act itself contemplates interest. The argument that Section 34 CPC caps MACT interest is contested and not settled law across all jurisdictions.

adverse.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
adverse.principle: Interest at 7.5% per annum is sufficient; 9% is excessive, following the Supreme Court in Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corporation v. Section Raj Priya.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this to argue that even 9% is too high and should be reduced to 7.5%, relying on a Supreme Court decision (Raj Priya) that allowed 7.5% keeping in view the bank rate.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Raj Priya did not lay down 7.5% as a universal cap — it was a fact-specific decision. Claimants can argue that 9% has been consistently awarded by numerous tribunals and High Courts (docs 022, 041, 010, 034) and remains the standard. The Kaushnuma Begum SC authority endorsing 9% is also binding.

adverse.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
adverse.principle: Interest at 7% per annum is a 'proper rate'.
adverse.risk_to_client: Insurers will cite this Allahabad High Court judgment to argue that 7% is judicially approved as 'proper', supporting a reduction from 9%.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court in doc_018 did not engage in any detailed analysis of the interest rate — it merely stated that the rate was 'proper' in a single sentence. It is not a considered ruling on the appropriate rate and carries less weight than the Supreme Court's guidance in Kaushnuma Begum endorsing 9%.
adverse.quote: The interest is also awarded at the proper rate of 7% per annum, chargeable from the date of petition till the date of actual payment.

priority_arguments: Lead with Kaushnuma Begum (via doc_034) — the Supreme Court has held that 9% is reasonable given RBI policy and bank rates, and this remains good law.
Point to the consistent pattern: 9% was awarded in 2001 (doc_034), 2016 (doc_041), and 2018 (docs 022, 010) — this is the settled rate across multiple tribunals and states.
Argue that the 6% rate in Soma Devi (doc_004) is an outlier from a single High Court judge, not binding precedent, and contradicts the Supreme Court's view in Kaushnuma Begum.
Distinguish doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) as a Karnataka-specific MACT decision applying Section 34 CPC — this is not the law across all states and is contrary to the weight of authority.
Emphasise that interest uniformly runs from the date of filing of the petition (not the accident date) — this is consistent across all judgments and should not be disturbed.

If the insurer argues for a lower rate, counter that the claimant should not bear the risk of fluctuating economic conditions; the compensation is meant to be 'just' and the rate should reflect the claimant's loss of use of the money, not the bank's deposit rate.
strategy.compensation_range: Interest at 9% per annum from the date of filing of the petition till realization is the most strongly supported position. If the court follows the downward trend, 7.5% or 7% is possible. 6% is the floor based on this corpus but is the least likely outcome given it is contradicted by Supreme Court authority.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The corpus shows a hierarchy: 9% (most common, supported by Kaushnuma Begum SC) > 7.5% (supported by Raj Priya SC) > 7% (Allahabad HC) > 6% (Himachal HC and Karnataka MACT). The starting date is uniformly the date of filing of the petition, not the accident date.
risks: The Himachal Pradesh High Court in Soma Devi (doc_004, 2020) reduced interest to 6%, and insurers will aggressively cite this as the most recent High Court authority on point.

The Karnataka High Court's Vijay Ishwar Jadhav line (applied in doc_024, 2024) holds that Section 34 CPC caps MACT interest at 6% — this is the most recent judgment in the corpus and directly adverse.
The general downward trend in interest rates may influence courts to reduce rates further, especially if the matter is heard in 2025-26.
If the claimant delayed filing the petition, the insurer may argue that interest should run from a later date or at a reduced rate.
Some courts may treat the interest rate as discretionary and not bound by precedent, leading to unpredictability.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Claimants should seek 9% per annum from the date of filing of the petition till realization, citing Kaushnuma Begum (via doc_034) and the consistent line of MACT decisions (docs 022, 041, 010). If the insurer cites Soma Devi (doc_004) or Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024), distinguish them as non-binding High Court/MACT decisions that contradict Supreme Court authority. In Karnataka, the Vijay Ishwar Jadhav precedent creates a specific risk that requires separate briefing.

caveats: doc_001 (United India Insurance v. Neelam Devi, 2023, Punjab & Haryana HC) — outcome 'mixed'. This judgment deals with income assessment methodology (DC rates vs minimum wages) and pay-and-recover rights for licence defects. It does not discuss interest rates at all and is irrelevant to the interest rate question.

doc_014 (Shivlal v. Rukmabai, 1985, MP HC) — outcome 'insurer'. This judgment deals with gratuitous passenger liability under the 1939 Motor Vehicles Act. It does not discuss interest rates and is irrelevant to the interest rate question.
The corpus does not contain any Supreme Court judgment directly ruling on the interest rate post-Pranay Sethi (2017). Practitioners should check for any Supreme Court ruling after 2020 on this point.

None of the judgments in the corpus discuss interest on the enhanced portion of compensation separately (i.e., whether interest on the enhanced amount runs from the date of the claim petition or from the date of the appellate order). This may be relevant in appeal scenarios.

The corpus does not contain any judgment awarding interest at a rate higher than 9% (the original 12% in doc_034 was reduced on appeal). Claimants seeking more than 9% will find no support in this corpus.
